reasoning: Set A is the better plan. Both sets follow the same discipline (interface task, spines, wiring, system task) and both have detailed contracts. The difference is in RL depth and accuracy. A gives each stage a ladder that teaches its concept: tabular Q-learning, then DQN, then a CNN on the full grid, with ablations; REINFORCE against PPO, with a library PPO comparison; then fixed opponents, naive co-learning and opponent-pool self-play, with cross-play tables and ratings. A's numeric test cases check out where I recomputed them (GAE 1.3775, Q-update 0.009, swim vector (0.0144, 0.0192), catch distances), and it keeps truncation separate from termination for bootstrapping. B has strong ideas of its own: hand-derived check worlds that gate every training batch, a paired permutation test with Holm correction, and replay by re-simulation. But B's tests contradict its own spec in several places. The fish score is tested as 'hits per fish, lower is better' while the spec says mean steps survived, higher is better. One test expects hit fish to respawn although the spec says they leave the episode. Another expects '2 predators' when the spec has one. A timing test allows a 90-minute batch against a 60-minute requirement. B's milestone split also has a leftover-looking M2 that bundles finishing the DQN, replay, the reference check and the write-up, and task IDs run out of order (T13 after T15, T25/T26 before T24). A has weaknesses too: one huge 31-task milestone per stage, an M1 interface that freezes M2/M3 fields, step tables that list classes the entry function never calls, a boundary list in CONSTRAINTS that no longer matches the architecture, and a fish test that contradicts EVAL-07. On structure, B is somewhat more readable for a solo learner.

strengths: Each stage has a ladder that isolates one concept, with ablations (no memory, no target copy, no exploration) and a library reference at each stage
Closed-form golden cases cited to Sutton & Barto and Schulman et al.; the ones I recomputed are correct
Contract types are code shapes with invariants, fixtures and cases; truncation and termination are kept separate for bootstrapping
Self-play design is concrete: opponent pool with a latest share, 10 generations, cross-play table, ratings and a fixed panel
weaknesses: One 31-task milestone per stage; M1 freezes RunSettings and Env fields that only M2/M3 use
PL-01's step table lists 16 rows (environment and agent classes) that the entry function never calls, so it doesn't read as a call path
Stale bits: the 'deliberately revised core' framing against AD-09's batch-first-from-M1 decision, and a CONSTRAINTS boundary list that omits selfplay/evaluate dependencies
The Snake spine packet (M1-T13) leaves out the SNAKE requirement text and relies on the test cases alone

strengths: Check worlds with hand-derived best actions gate every training batch, a strong defence against silent RL bugs
The paired permutation test with Holm correction is fully specified; replay works by deterministic re-simulation, with side-by-side view and video
The brief and spec read naturally for a solo learner; the write-up feature supports explaining why it works
Opponent pool and pairing grid cover self-play; architecture boundaries match CONSTRAINTS
weaknesses: Tests contradict the spec on the fish score's metric and direction, on fish respawn, and on predator count
